title: Mobile App Developer (Android / Flutter)
summary: Mobile developers build the apps people use on their phones. You can go native Android with Kotlin, or use Flutter with Dart to build for Android and iOS from one codebase. This path suits students who like building things they can hold and show friends.

sources.title: Mobile Application Security Cheat Sheet – OWASP

nodes.title: Programming basics and object-oriented thinking
nodes.summary: Before touching app frameworks, get comfortable with variables, loops, functions, classes and objects in one language. Java is a good start because its ideas carry over to both Kotlin and Dart.
nodes.proof: Write a small console program, such as a student marks manager, that uses classes, lists and file saving.

nodes.title: Git and GitHub
nodes.summary: Keep every app in Git from the first day, commit often and push to GitHub. Recruiters and teams look at your repos, and Git saves you when an experiment breaks your project.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education – MIT

nodes.proof: All your practice apps are on GitHub with READMEs and a history of small, clearly described commits.

nodes.title: Choose a track: native Android or Flutter
nodes.summary: Native Android uses Kotlin and Android's own tools; Flutter uses Dart and targets Android and iOS from one codebase. Look at job posts near you, try a small tutorial in each, then commit to one for at least six months.
nodes.proof: A short note in your notebook or repo explaining which track you chose and why, based on job posts you read.

nodes.title: Kotlin or Dart
nodes.summary: Learn the language of your track: Kotlin for native Android or Dart for Flutter. Focus on null safety, collections, classes and asynchronous code, since apps constantly wait on networks and storage.
nodes.proof: Solve 20 small exercises in Kotlin or Dart, including at least three that use asynchronous code.

nodes.title: Screens, navigation and state
nodes.summary: Build user interfaces with your track's UI toolkit (Jetpack Compose on Android, widgets in Flutter), move between screens, handle user input, and manage app state so the screen updates correctly.
nodes.proof: Build a three-screen app, such as a habit tracker, with a list, a detail view and a form that updates the list.

nodes.title: Networking, APIs and local storage
nodes.summary: Most apps load data from a server over HTTP and keep some of it on the phone so they still work on a weak connection. Learn how HTTP and REST APIs work, how to parse JSON, and how to store data locally.

resources.title: Overview of HTTP – MDN Web Docs

nodes.proof: Extend your app to load data from a public API, show loading and error states, and keep the last result for offline use.

sources.title: Overview of HTTP – MDN Web Docs

nodes.title: Mobile app security basics
nodes.summary: Never hard-code secret keys in the app, store sensitive data with the platform's secure storage, use HTTPS only, and ask for as few permissions as possible. Users trust apps with personal data on their phones.

resources.title: Mobile Application Security Cheat Sheet – OWASP

nodes.proof: Review your own app against the OWASP mobile cheat sheet and list each issue you fixed in the README.

sources.title: Mobile Application Security Cheat Sheet – OWASP

nodes.title: Build and release a complete app
nodes.summary: Build one useful app from idea to release, such as a campus events or expense tracker app, with several screens, an API, offline storage and a clean design. Share an installable build and the code.
nodes.proof: A public repo with screenshots, a short screen recording and an installable build or store listing link that others can try.

sources.title: What You Can Do to Prepare – The Odin Project

nodes.title: Interviews and applying
nodes.summary: Prepare to demo your app and explain how it handles state, data and errors. Revise programming and data structure basics for coding rounds, learn the usual hiring steps, and apply steadily.

resources.title: Preparing to Interview and Interviewing – The Odin Project

nodes.proof: A five-minute demo video of your app, a one-page resume, and three mock interviews completed with notes.

sources.title: What Companies Want – The Odin Project
